title: ASIC Regulatory Guide 38 The hawking prohibition
legislative_instrument: RG 38 (issued 23 September 2021, updated March 2024); guidance on Corporations Act ss992A and 992AA
licence: ASIC regulatory guide (copyright ASIC). Paraphrased only; consult the published guide.
verification_notes: Checked against the published PDF (rg38-published-23-september-2021-20240328.pdf) downloaded from asic.gov.au on 2026-10-19. Document history: in March 2024 ASIC deleted the previous RG 38.10 and renumbered the following two paragraphs, and updated some legislative instrument references; citations in this file use the current (post-March 2024) numbering, so older internal references to RG 38.10 to RG 38.12 may be off by one. Statutory text of s992A cross-checked against Corporations Act Compilation No. 149 (consent requirements in s992A(5), 6 week and 12 week periods in s992A(5)(g), strict liability in s992A(9)). Penalty figures (60 penalty units or 6 months imprisonment for individuals, 600 penalty units for bodies corporate) are as stated in RG 38.127 and were not cross-checked against Schedule 3. RG 38 commenced with the new prohibition on 5 October 2021. Private health insurance products are not financial products (s765A(1)(c)), so the hawking prohibition does not apply to them, although telemarketing of PHI remains subject to the Australian Consumer Law and Do Not Call Register rules.

summary: RG 38 explains the hawking prohibition in s992A of the Corporations Act, which from 5 October 2021 prohibits offering, or requesting or inviting a retail client to apply for or buy, a financial product (including general and life insurance) in the course of or because of an unsolicited real-time contact. Contact is unsolicited unless the consumer gave prior consent that is positive, voluntary and clear, covers the product, is used in any form specified, is no more than 6 weeks old (12 weeks where a medical examination is needed) and has not been withdrawn. The prohibition is technology neutral and expressly covers chat-bots and other AI sales tools. Breach is a strict liability offence and gives the consumer a right to return the product for a full premium refund.

clauses.heading: The hawking prohibition
clauses.text: Under s992A(1), an offeror must not offer a financial product for issue or sale to a retail client if the offer is made in the course of, or because of, an unsolicited contact. An offeror includes the issuer or seller and their agents or representatives, and the prohibition extends to requesting or inviting a retail client to ask or apply for, or buy, a product (RG 38.6). Giving an insurance quote or asking a consumer to complete an application form will generally be an offer, request or invitation (RG 38.42). Failure to comply is a strict liability offence and gives the consumer a right of return (RG 38.10).
subclauses: RG 38.6: offerors include issuers, sellers, agents and representatives; requests and invitations are covered.
RG 38.17: applies only to retail clients.
RG 38.20: does not apply to offers made in the course of personal advice by a person subject to the best interests duty.
RG 38.21 to RG 38.22: add-on insurance is outside the prohibition during the deferral period, but generally subject to it otherwise, including where exempt from the deferred sales model.
RG 38.27: contacting existing clients about products they already hold is permitted if no new product is offered.
RG 38.42: quotes and requests to complete application forms are generally offers, requests or invitations.
RG 38.43: giving factual product information in real time without an offer, request or invitation is not hawking.
clauses.notes: Statutory basis s992A(1). Any outbound or proactive AI agent (voice, chat or messaging) must not move from information to an offer, quote or invitation to apply unless a valid consent covers that product. The current prohibition commenced 5 October 2021. Maximum penalties per RG 38.127: individuals 60 penalty units or 6 months imprisonment or both; bodies corporate 600 penalty units. Not applicable to private health insurance products.

clauses.heading: Meaning of 'unsolicited contact', including chat-bots
clauses.text: Unsolicited contact is contact by telephone, face-to-face, or any other real-time interaction in the nature of a discussion or conversation, to which the consumer did not validly consent (s992A(4)). The prohibition is technology neutral and covers instant messaging and AI tools such as chat-bots (RG 38.36). It cannot be avoided by engaging a third party, including a vendor that builds an AI sales tool; the person commissioning the chat-bot, or under whose licence it operates, is responsible for its offers (RG 38.37). Real-time means the parties respond to each other continuously or there is an expectation of immediate response, whether verbal or written; whether text messages qualify depends on the circumstances (RG 38.38).
subclauses: RG 38.34: forms of contact: telephone, face-to-face, or other real-time conversational interaction.
RG 38.35: non-real-time communications (for example mail-outs) may invite consumers to request future contact, but any later offer must comply.
RG 38.36: technology neutral, including instant messages and AI chat-bots.
RG 38.37: licensee responsible for chat-bots operated under its licence, including third-party built tools.
RG 38.38: real-time includes written channels where an immediate response is expected.
RG 38.44: brochures, TV and radio advertising are outside the prohibition.
RG 38.45: an offer made later by email can still breach if it is made because of an unsolicited real-time contact.
RG 38.48 to RG 38.56: causal link between the unsolicited contact and the later offer.
clauses.notes: ASIC expressly treats AI chat-bots as within scope and makes the licensee responsible. A chat-bot that initiates a conversation (for example a proactive website pop-up, in-app nudge or outbound message expecting a reply) and then quotes or invites an application is at high risk unless prior consent is in place. Where the customer initiates the chat, the contact is not unsolicited, but offers must stay within the scope of what the customer asked about.

clauses.heading: Valid consent: positive, voluntary and clear
clauses.text: Contact is unsolicited unless the consumer first gave consent that is positive, voluntary and clear, such that a reasonable person would understand the consumer was consenting to the contact (s992A(5)(d) to (e)). Consent must be given before the contact and not withdrawn (RG 38.58), cannot be elicited by the offeror during an unsolicited contact (RG 38.59), and if it specifies a form of contact only that form may be used (RG 38.60). Positive consent requires an active step such as the consumer calling or submitting an online form, not silence or failure to act (RG 38.64). The offer must be for a product the consent covers or that is reasonably within its scope (RG 38.85). Consent lasts 6 weeks, or up to 12 weeks if the consumer agrees and a medical examination is reasonably needed (RG 38.111). Consumers may vary or withdraw consent at any time in any form (RG 38.115).
subclauses: RG 38.57: contact without consent is unsolicited.
RG 38.58: consent must precede the contact and not have been withdrawn.
RG 38.59: offerors cannot elicit consent during the contact.
RG 38.60: honour any specified form of contact.
RG 38.63 to RG 38.67: positive and voluntary; silence or inaction is not consent.
RG 38.69 to RG 38.71: clear consent understood by a reasonable person; silence is generally not enough.
RG 38.85 to RG 38.90: scope of consent and closely related products.
RG 38.111 to RG 38.113: 6 week validity (12 weeks for medical examination); a new consent must meet all criteria.
RG 38.115 to RG 38.116: variation or withdrawal in any form must be honoured.
RG 38.122 to RG 38.124: keep records of consents and their scope.
clauses.notes: Statutory basis s992A(4)(b) and (5). An AI sales agent needs a consent ledger: source, timestamp, products covered, permitted channels, and withdrawal status. Before any offer the agent must check the consent is current (within 6 weeks, or 12 weeks for products needing a medical examination, which is relevant to life insurance), in scope and not withdrawn, and it must stop immediately if the customer withdraws or narrows consent mid-conversation.

clauses.section_name: F: Consequences of breaching the hawking prohibition
clauses.heading: Right of return and refund
clauses.text: If the hawking prohibition is breached, the consumer may return the product and obtain a refund (s992AA). The right is exercisable within 1 month after the end of any statutory cooling-off period, or otherwise within 1 month and 14 days after issue or sale (RG 38.132 to RG 38.133). For insurance products the refund is of all premiums paid (RG 38.144). ASIC considers it good practice to tell consumers about the right of return (RG 38.130).
subclauses: RG 38.127: strict liability offence with stated maximum penalties.
RG 38.128: consumers may also seek civil remedies under s1324.
RG 38.132 to RG 38.133: timing of the right of return.
RG 38.144: insurance refunds cover all premiums paid.
RG 38.147: where one breach is identified, consider whether the same conduct or compliance failure caused further breaches (see RG 277 Consumer remediation).
clauses.notes: Hawking breaches by an AI agent can lead to product returns with full premium refunds and may be reportable under s912D. Agent logs must let the insurer reconstruct whether each sale was made under a valid consent.
